ny_lost_t.blurb: Lost T is a small cliff in the southern Adirondacks, set back in the woods above Chub Lake. Twenty-four routes are spread across the wall, mostly traditional lines on crack systems with a handful of bolted ones. Faces run roughly forty to eighty feet tall. Grades start near 5.5 and top out in the low 5.12s, but the bulk of the climbing sits between 5.7 and 5.10, which makes it a friendly place to build trad skills. Most lines can be rigged for top-roping, and a few bolted starts are meant to be stick-clipped. It is quiet and forested, with a short uphill walk in.

ny_lost_hunters.blurb: Lost Hunters is a steep backcountry cliff on Sherman Mountain in the southern Adirondacks, a longer hike in than its neighbor Lost T. The main wall faces west and is sheer to overhanging, with face climbing between a couple of crack lines; smaller walls off to the left face southwest. Twenty-two routes, about two-thirds bolted and the rest trad, begin around 5.8 and climb to 5.13. Most of the grades cluster in the 5.11 to 5.13 range, so this is a destination for strong climbers rather than beginners. Expect a remote, uncrowded setting with some of the better hard face climbing in the region.

ny_steel_bridge_boulders.blurb: Steel Bridge Boulders is a cluster of blocks just north of the Trapps bridge in the Shawangunks, a short stroll from the road. The stone is hard quartz conglomerate. About two dozen problems are here, and the majority are easy, in the V0 range, which makes it a handy warm-up spot and a good one for newer boulderers. A scattering of harder lines climbs through V4 to V8, and a few much harder test pieces reach into the V11 and V12 range. A big boulder with tall highball problems adds some serious options. Landings and heights vary, so scout before pulling on.

ny_doug_s_roof.blurb: Doug's Roof is a bouldering spot in the Trapps section of the Shawangunks, about a four-minute walk along the carriage road from the bridge. A large overhanging roof by the roadside gives it a covered feel, so it is a favorite warm-up area and a place to keep climbing when showers pass. Roughly twenty problems are here, and half are very easy, V0 or below, with a smattering of V1 to V2 and a few harder bulge, traverse and crack lines reaching V6 and V7. The hard conglomerate gives positive holds and many traverse variations. Good for beginners and for loosening up.

ny_area_1.blurb: Area 1 is the biggest group of boulders at the roadside bouldering spot near Canada Lake in the southern Adirondacks, set northeast of the warm-up boulders. About two dozen problems are here, most of them easy to moderate, between V0 and V3, with a smaller number in the V4 to V5 range and a pair of much harder lines near V7 and V8. The boulders are a short walk from the pullout, which keeps logistics simple. It suits a relaxed session for mixed-ability groups, with a few projects for stronger climbers. Bring pads for the landings.

ny_dihedrals_the.blurb: The Dihedrals is a small cliff on the north bank of the Mohawk River at Little Falls, a convenient option for climbers in central New York. The rock is a good-quality syenite, and some patches have a smooth dark finish that bakes in summer sun. Twenty-three routes, mostly trad, with a few sport lines and a top-rope or two, go from about 5.6 up to the low 5.13 range. None is taller than about sixty-five feet, and cracks take solid gear. The setting is industrial, with trains rolling close to the base, so expect noise and little solitude.

ny_pitchoff_chimney_cliff.blurb: Pitchoff Chimney Cliff is the busiest crag near Keene in the Adirondacks, on the road through Cascade Pass with views across the lakes. The rock is excellent, with cracks and faces in both directions, and the gear is generally good. Twenty-two routes, nearly all trad, plus a couple of sport lines and a top-rope, run from the 5.6 range to 5.12, with the greatest concentration from 5.8 to 5.11. Several classics are multi-pitch, making it a good objective for a half day. A short walk in and roadside access draw crowds on weekends.

ny_potter_mountain_cliff.blurb: Potter Mountain Cliff is one of the largest walls in the Silver Lake complex in the northern Adirondacks, sitting just under the summit ridge. It is known for long face climbing on clean, textured stone. Twenty-four routes, about sixty percent sport and the rest trad, concentrate in the 5.10 range, with a few at 5.8 to 5.9 and some in the 5.11 to 5.12 range. Several lines go multi-pitch, and double ropes are needed to get down. The wall heats up in warm weather, so cooler days are better. The walk in follows logging roads and a faint cairned path, and navigation is easy to botch.
